We enjoy solving real-world problems, sharing ideas, and turning creative concepts into practical solutions. We are looking for enthusiastic teammates with skills in programming, machine learning, data analysis, web development, UI/UX design, science, or engineering. summary:
PyroSync is a web application that brings NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS fire observations together into a consistent burning activity calendar. It addresses a central challenge in long-term fire monitoring: changes in satellite resolution, sensitivity, and coverage can appear as changes in fire activity.

Our harmonization pipeline removes duplicate observations, matches detections across sensors, corrects MODIS viewing-angle effects, and adjusts detection counts for changes in satellite observation coverage. An interactive dashboard lets users explore regional fire patterns from 2000–2025, compare raw and harmonized data, identify unusual months, and export results as CSV or GeoJSON. Uncertainty estimates and quality flags help users interpret the results and their limitations.

By making satellite differences visible and reducing their influence on historical comparisons, PyroSync helps researchers, land managers, and emergency planners distinguish fire activity changes from measurement effects. This supports better-informed decisions about seasonal preparedness, resource allocation, and long-term fire management.
details:
PyroSync turns fragmented satellite fire observations into an interactive burning activity calendar. Built for the “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots” challenge, it helps users explore when and where fire activity occurs, compare seasons, and identify unusual patterns across regions. It combines historical NASA FIRMS records from 2000–2025 with access to near-real-time observations.

The central problem is that satellite detections are not directly comparable. MODIS observes fires at approximately 1 km resolution, while VIIRS provides finer 375 m observations and detects smaller fires. As new satellites join the observing fleet, detection counts can rise even without a corresponding increase in fire activity. Simply combining these records can therefore create misleading trends.

Our seven-stage processing pipeline addresses these differences. It ingests FIRMS data, removes overlapping scan detections, consolidates repeated observations within each satellite family, and matches MODIS and VIIRS observations in space and time using an H3 hexagonal index. Multiple VIIRS pixels within a matched MODIS footprint are grouped so their fire radiative power can be compared at a more consistent spatial scale. The pipeline then applies a viewing-angle correction to MODIS fire radiative power and normalizes monthly detection counts for changes in satellite observation coverage, using MODIS as the reference.

The web application makes this processing understandable and useful. Users can select a region and period, explore hotspot maps and monthly calendars, compare sensor contributions, and examine anomalies against historical activity. A Raw/Harmonized toggle reveals how processing changes the results. Diagnostic panels explain duplicate removal, normalization, uncertainty, and data quality. Users can also compare alternative fusion models, download CSV or GeoJSON files, and generate printable regional briefings.

PyroSync’s intended impact is to support more informed fire research, land management, and seasonal preparedness. Researchers can investigate historical patterns with fewer distortions from sensor changes. Land managers and emergency planners can identify unusually active periods and use historical context to inform resource planning. Exportable results make the project useful beyond the dashboard.

We developed the processing engine and backend in Rust, using Axum and Tokio for the API and asynchronous services. The frontend uses React and TypeScript, with Vite for development and production builds. H3 supports spatial indexing, Docker provides reproducible deployment, and automated Rust and frontend tests support reliability. The system uses existing satellite observations and requires no custom sensing hardware.

Our creative contribution is the combination of scientific processing and an interface that lets users inspect its effects. The Footprint Lens explains why one MODIS detection may correspond to several VIIRS pixels, while the comparison views make measurement differences tangible.

Throughout development, we considered spatial resolution, observation timing, duplicate detections, changing satellite coverage, viewing geometry, performance, accessibility, and reproducibility. We also made limitations visible: harmonized values are estimates, hotspot detections do not equal individual fires, and periods with insufficient comparability are flagged. This transparency helps users judge where the results can support a decision and where additional evidence is needed.
